nodes/book_basics/desc.en: Free. Was already in the box in the tent: planting, fire, rope, the first tools.

nodes/book_village/desc.en: Timber, clay, walls and roofs — how the village builds.

nodes/book_kitchen/desc.en: Stoves, bread, butter, honey and salt.

nodes/book_soil/desc.en: Rotation, seasons, frost, ponds and trees.

nodes/book_smith/desc.en: Iron, anvils, nails and wind power.

nodes/book_cellar/desc.en: Presses, ferments, cheese, cellars and pickles.

nodes/book_glass/desc.en: Steel, glass, greenhouses and brick houses.

nodes/book_orchard/desc.en: Pruning, olives, pasta, hardwood and deep soil.

nodes/book_master/desc.en: Worms, seed saving, saffron, master baking, wind pumps.

nodes/book_cart/desc.en: Comes with the travelling merchant. Sells the books your library has room for.

nodes/library_box/desc.en: Holds 2 books. The Little Farm Book was already in it.

nodes/library_shelf/desc.en: Holds 5 books. Reading 10% faster. Needs 5 cards learned.

nodes/library_bookcase/desc.en: Holds 10 books. Reading 20% faster. Needs 15 cards learned.

nodes/library_room/desc.en: A quiet room of your own: all 12 books, reading 30% faster, and a cosy chair (+0.5 energy per Rest answer). Needs 30 cards learned.

nodes/k_wheat/desc.en: Opening the book. A seed needs soil, water and time.

nodes/k_wheat/page.en: Every seed needs three things to grow: soil, water and time. Farmers sow wheat seeds in loose soil and water them. The green stalks grow tall, turn golden, and then they are cut. Each stalk gives grain, to eat or to sow again, and a dry stem called straw.

nodes/k_wheat/questions/0/q.en: What three things does a seed need to grow?

nodes/k_wheat/questions/0/why.en: With soil, water and enough time, a seed can sprout and grow.

nodes/k_wheat/questions/1/q.en: How can you tell your wheat is ready to cut?

nodes/k_wheat/questions/1/why.en: Wheat turns golden when the grain is ripe and ready to harvest.

nodes/k_wheat/questions/2/q.en: What two things does each wheat stalk give you?

nodes/k_wheat/questions/2/why.en: The top gives grain to eat or sow, and the dry stem is straw.

nodes/k_fire/desc.en: Fire needs three things: fuel, air and heat (fire triangle). Build it inside a ring of stones, start with dry twigs before thicker sticks, never leave it alone, put it out with water or soil..

nodes/k_fire/page.en: A fire needs three things: fuel to burn, air, and heat. Build it inside a ring of stones, and light small dry twigs before you add thicker sticks. Never leave a fire alone. To put it out, pour on water or cover it with soil, which keeps the air away.

nodes/k_fire/questions/0/q.en: What three things does every fire need?

nodes/k_fire/questions/0/why.en: Take away the fuel, the air or the heat, and the fire goes out.

nodes/k_fire/questions/1/q.en: Your big sticks won't catch fire. What should you light first?

nodes/k_fire/questions/1/why.en: Small dry twigs catch fire easily and then help the bigger sticks burn.

nodes/k_fire/questions/2/q.en: Why does covering a fire with soil put it out?

nodes/k_fire/questions/2/why.en: A fire needs air, so covering it with soil makes it go out.

nodes/k_fire/questions/2/answers/0.en: The soil keeps the air away

nodes/k_fire/questions/2/answers/1.en: The soil makes the fire hotter

nodes/k_fire/questions/2/answers/2.en: The soil burns up like fuel

nodes/k_roots/desc.en: Carrots and onions are plants whose roots/bulbs we eat.

nodes/k_roots/page.en: With carrots and onions, we eat the part under the ground: a carrot's root and an onion's round bulb. Their green leaves above the ground use sunlight to make food for the plant. They grow more slowly than leafy plants like lettuce. Pull them up when the green tops are big.

nodes/k_roots/questions/0/q.en: Which part of a carrot do we eat?

nodes/k_roots/questions/0/why.en: The orange part we eat is the carrot's root, which grows underground.

nodes/k_roots/questions/1/q.en: What do the green leaves of a carrot do?

nodes/k_roots/questions/1/why.en: Leaves use sunlight to make food for the whole plant, even the root.

nodes/k_roots/questions/1/answers/1.en: Soak up rain for the root

nodes/k_roots/questions/2/q.en: How can you tell your carrots are ready to pull?

nodes/k_roots/questions/2/why.en: Big green tops mean the root below has had time to grow big too.

nodes/k_roots/questions/2/answers/1.en: The leaves are still small and new

nodes/k_rope/desc.en: Rope is made by twisting plant fibres (from tough weed stems, flax, or straw) into strands and twisting the strands together the other way so the rope does not unwind.

nodes/k_rope/page.en: Rope is made from fibres, the thin, tough threads inside plant stems like flax or straw. First you twist the fibres into strands. Then you twist the strands together the other way, so the rope does not unwind. The more strands you use, the stronger the rope.

nodes/k_rope/questions/0/q.en: Why twist the strands together the other way?

nodes/k_rope/questions/0/why.en: Twisting the opposite way locks the strands, so the rope holds together.

nodes/k_rope/questions/0/answers/0.en: So the rope does not unwind

nodes/k_rope/questions/1/q.en: You need rope to lift a heavy bucket. What makes it stronger?

nodes/k_rope/questions/1/why.en: Each extra strand shares the pull, so the rope gets stronger.

nodes/k_rope/questions/2/why.en: Fibres from plants like flax or straw are twisted to make rope.

nodes/k_rope/questions/2/answers/1.en: Thin twigs tied together in knots

nodes/k_tools/desc.en: The first tools: a sharp flake of stone becomes a knife.

nodes/k_tools/page.en: The first tools were made of stone. A sharp flake chipped off a stone makes a knife. Tie a stone to a wooden handle with rope to make an axe; the handle lets you swing much harder. People used stone tools for a very, very long time, called the Stone Age.

nodes/k_tools/questions/0/q.en: Why tie a stone axe head onto a handle?

nodes/k_tools/questions/0/why.en: A handle works like a longer arm, so each swing hits much harder.

nodes/k_tools/questions/0/answers/0.en: So you can swing much harder

nodes/k_tools/questions/0/answers/1.en: So the stone stays sharp forever

nodes/k_tools/questions/1/q.en: How were the very first knives made?

nodes/k_tools/questions/1/why.en: People chipped a sharp flake off a stone and used it to cut.

nodes/k_tools/questions/1/answers/0.en: From a sharp flake of stone

nodes/k_tools/questions/1/answers/1.en: From melted iron poured into a mould

nodes/k_tools/questions/2/q.en: What do we call the long time when people used stone tools?

nodes/k_tools/questions/2/why.en: People used stone tools for so long that we call it the Stone Age.

nodes/k_weeds/desc.en: Weeds are wild plants that grow where we do not want them.

nodes/k_weeds/page.en: Weeds are wild plants that grow where we don't want them. They steal water, light and food from our crops. Their seeds blow in on the wind and can wait in the soil for years. Pull weeds out with their roots, and use a border or a cover of straw to keep new ones away.

nodes/k_weeds/questions/0/q.en: Why are weeds bad for your crops?

nodes/k_weeds/questions/0/why.en: Weeds take the water, light and food that your crops need.

nodes/k_weeds/questions/0/answers/0.en: They steal water, light and food

nodes/k_weeds/questions/0/answers/1.en: They make the soil much too loose

nodes/k_weeds/questions/1/q.en: You pulled a weed, but it grew back. What went wrong?

nodes/k_weeds/questions/1/why.en: If the roots stay in the ground, the weed can grow again.

nodes/k_weeds/questions/1/answers/0.en: Its roots stayed in the soil

nodes/k_weeds/questions/1/answers/1.en: You pulled it on a sunny day

nodes/k_weeds/questions/2/q.en: Your bed is clean now. How can you keep new weeds away?

nodes/k_weeds/questions/2/why.en: A straw cover or a border stops many weed seeds from growing.

nodes/k_weeds/questions/2/answers/1.en: Water the bare soil every day

nodes/k_water/desc.en: A well reaches water stored underground (groundwater) that came from rain soaking into the soil.

nodes/k_water/page.en: Rain soaks down through the soil and is stored deep underground. This water is called groundwater. A well is a deep hole that reaches it, and a deeper well reaches more water. A winch, which is a roller with a handle, makes lifting the heavy bucket much easier.

nodes/k_water/questions/0/q.en: Where does the water in a well come from?

nodes/k_water/questions/0/why.en: Rain soaks into the soil and collects deep underground as groundwater.

nodes/k_water/questions/0/answers/0.en: Rain that soaked into the ground

nodes/k_water/questions/0/answers/1.en: The sea, flowing under the farm

nodes/k_water/questions/0/answers/2.en: Ice melting at the bottom of the hole

nodes/k_water/questions/1/q.en: Your well keeps running dry. What could help?

nodes/k_water/questions/1/why.en: A deeper well reaches more of the water stored underground.

nodes/k_water/questions/2/q.en: What does a winch help you do?

nodes/k_water/questions/2/why.en: Turning the winch handle winds up the rope, so lifting is easier.

nodes/k_soil/desc.en: Roots need air and water in the soil.

nodes/k_soil/page.en: Roots need air and water in the soil to grow. Digging breaks up hard soil, so roots can grow deep and more plants fit in one bed. Worms help too, because their tunnels loosen the soil. But stamping on a bed packs it hard again.

nodes/k_soil/questions/0/q.en: Why do roots grow better in loose soil?

nodes/k_soil/questions/0/why.en: Loose soil has room for air and water, and roots can push down deep.

nodes/k_soil/questions/0/answers/1.en: Loose soil is warmer in winter

nodes/k_soil/questions/1/q.en: Which little animal helps loosen the soil?

nodes/k_soil/questions/1/why.en: Worms dig tunnels as they move, which loosens the soil.

nodes/k_soil/questions/2/q.en: Your friend keeps walking on your bed. What happens to the soil?

nodes/k_soil/questions/2/why.en: Feet squeeze the soil tight, so roots struggle to grow.

nodes/k_ash/desc.en: Wood ash from a fire contains minerals (like potassium) that plants need.

nodes/k_ash/page.en: Wood ash from the fire holds minerals, like potassium, that plants need. Sprinkle a little on your beds to feed your crops. Plants growing close together need extra food, called fertilizer. But be careful: too much ash can harm plants.

nodes/k_ash/questions/0/q.en: Why sprinkle wood ash on your beds?

nodes/k_ash/questions/0/why.en: Ash holds minerals like potassium, which help plants grow.

nodes/k_ash/questions/0/answers/0.en: It has minerals that feed plants

nodes/k_ash/questions/0/answers/2.en: It helps the soil hold on to rain

nodes/k_ash/questions/1/q.en: Your bed is packed with plants. What do they need more of?

nodes/k_ash/questions/1/why.en: Many plants close together share the soil's food, so they need extra.

nodes/k_ash/questions/2/q.en: How much ash should you put on a bed?

nodes/k_ash/questions/2/why.en: A little ash feeds plants, but too much can harm them.

nodes/k_chickens/desc.en: Hens eat grain and seeds, drink water every day, need a dry coop with straw to sleep safe from foxes, and lay eggs.

nodes/k_chickens/page.en: Hens eat grain and seeds, and they scratch the ground to find bugs. They need fresh water every day and a dry coop with straw, where they sleep safe from foxes. Hens lay eggs, and a hen does not need a rooster to lay them.

nodes/k_chickens/questions/0/q.en: Where should your hens sleep at night?

nodes/k_chickens/questions/0/why.en: A dry coop keeps hens cosy and safe from foxes.

nodes/k_chickens/questions/0/answers/0.en: In a dry coop with straw

nodes/k_chickens/questions/0/answers/1.en: Out in the open field all night

nodes/k_chickens/questions/1/q.en: Do hens need a rooster to lay eggs?

nodes/k_chickens/questions/1/why.en: A hen lays eggs whether or not there is a rooster.

nodes/k_chickens/questions/1/answers/0.en: No, hens lay eggs on their own

nodes/k_chickens/questions/1/answers/1.en: Yes, every egg needs a rooster

nodes/k_chickens/questions/2/q.en: Why do hens scratch at the ground?

nodes/k_chickens/questions/2/why.en: Hens scratch the soil to find tasty bugs and seeds.

nodes/k_birds/desc.en: Birds love freshly sown seeds and rabbits nibble young plants.

nodes/k_birds/page.en: Birds love to eat freshly sown seeds, and rabbits nibble young plants. A scarecrow looks like a person, so it frightens birds, but things that flap or move scare them even better. A fence keeps rabbits out. Remember: the more plants you grow, the more hungry visitors come.

nodes/k_birds/questions/0/q.en: Which scarecrow will keep birds away best?

nodes/k_birds/questions/0/why.en: Moving, flapping things scare birds better than a scarecrow that never moves.

nodes/k_birds/questions/1/q.en: Rabbits keep nibbling your young plants. What helps most?

nodes/k_birds/questions/1/why.en: A fence stops rabbits from reaching your plants.

nodes/k_birds/questions/2/q.en: You planted twice as many crops. What should you expect?

nodes/k_birds/questions/2/why.en: More plants mean more food, so more hungry visitors come.

nodes/k_birds/questions/2/answers/1.en: Fewer birds and rabbits than before

nodes/k_grinding/desc.en: Flour is grain ground into powder between two stones (a quern, later a mill).

nodes/k_grinding/page.en: Flour is grain that has been ground into powder. You crush the grain between two heavy stones called a quern; later, people built mills to do it. The hard outside of the grain, called bran, and the soft inside both get crushed. It takes lots of turning by hand, but then you can make bread and pancakes.

nodes/k_grinding/questions/0/q.en: How is grain turned into flour?

nodes/k_grinding/questions/0/why.en: Two heavy stones grind the grain until it becomes fine powder.

nodes/k_grinding/questions/0/answers/0.en: It is crushed between two stones

nodes/k_grinding/questions/0/answers/1.en: It is soaked in water for many days

nodes/k_grinding/questions/0/answers/2.en: It is dried in the sun

nodes/k_grinding/questions/1/why.en: Bran is the tough outer skin of each grain.

nodes/k_grinding/questions/1/answers/0.en: The hard outside of the grain

nodes/k_grinding/questions/1/answers/1.en: The soft inside of the grain

nodes/k_grinding/questions/2/q.en: Why is making flour by hand hard work?

nodes/k_grinding/questions/2/why.en: You turn the quern stone again and again to grind the grain.

nodes/k_grinding/questions/2/answers/0.en: The stone needs lots of turning

nodes/k_grinding/questions/2/answers/2.en: The grain has to be boiled first

nodes/k_market/desc.en: Buying and selling: things that take more work or are rare cost more.

nodes/k_market/page.en: At the market, people buy and sell. Things that are rare, or take lots of work to make, cost more. When you turn cheap things into something better, like flour into bread, it is worth more. A fair price is good for the buyer and the seller, and money is just a handy way to swap work.

nodes/k_market/questions/0/q.en: Why does a loaf of bread cost more than its flour?

nodes/k_market/questions/0/why.en: Turning flour into bread takes work, so the bread is worth more.

nodes/k_market/questions/1/why.en: A fair price is good for both people, so both are happy to trade.

nodes/k_market/questions/1/answers/0.en: It is good for buyer and seller

nodes/k_market/questions/1/answers/1.en: The seller gets as much as possible

nodes/k_market/questions/2/q.en: Only a few people sell honey. Why does it cost a lot?

nodes/k_market/questions/2/why.en: When something is rare, people pay more for the little there is.

nodes/k_timber/desc.en: A log can be split along the grain (the lines of the wood) into planks with an axe and wedges.

nodes/k_timber/page.en: Wood has lines running along it, called the grain. With an axe and wedges you can split a log along the grain into planks. A saw cuts thinner planks and wastes less wood. Wood is strongest along the grain, and trees take many years to grow, so never waste it.

nodes/k_timber/questions/0/q.en: What is the grain of wood?

nodes/k_timber/questions/0/why.en: Grain means the lines in wood, which show the way it splits.

nodes/k_timber/questions/0/answers/0.en: The lines that run along it

nodes/k_timber/questions/0/answers/1.en: The little seeds inside a log

nodes/k_timber/questions/1/q.en: Why use a saw for thin planks instead of an axe?

nodes/k_timber/questions/1/why.en: A saw cuts neat, thin planks, so more of the log gets used.

nodes/k_timber/questions/1/answers/2.en: A saw makes the tree grow back

nodes/k_timber/questions/2/q.en: Why should you never waste wood?

nodes/k_timber/questions/2/why.en: A tree needs many years to grow big enough for planks.

nodes/k_timber/questions/2/answers/0.en: Trees take many years to grow

nodes/k_timber/questions/2/answers/1.en: Wood is much heavier than stone

nodes/k_clay/desc.en: Clay is very fine, sticky earth.

nodes/k_clay/page.en: Clay is very fine, sticky earth that you can shape when it is wet. Unfired clay gets soft in the rain and crumbles. Baked in a very hot oven called a kiln, it turns hard for good, and water can't soften it again. That is how we make bricks and jars.

nodes/k_clay/questions/0/q.en: When is clay easiest to shape?

nodes/k_clay/questions/0/why.en: Wet clay is soft and sticky, so you can press it into shape.

nodes/k_clay/questions/1/q.en: Why are bricks fired in a kiln?

nodes/k_clay/questions/1/why.en: Firing makes clay hard for good, so water can't soften it.

nodes/k_clay/questions/1/answers/1.en: So they stay soft and sticky

nodes/k_clay/questions/1/answers/2.en: So they turn back into earth

nodes/k_clay/questions/2/q.en: Your unfired clay pot was left out in the rain. What happens?

nodes/k_clay/questions/2/why.en: Unfired clay soaks up rain and falls apart.

nodes/k_clay/questions/2/answers/1.en: It bakes as hard as a stone

nodes/k_charcoal/desc.en: Charcoal is wood heated with very little air so it does not burn up.

nodes/k_charcoal/page.en: Charcoal is made by heating wood with very little air, so it can't burn up. The water and smoke leave the wood, and the black part that stays behind is called carbon. Charcoal burns hotter and cleaner than wood, so smiths and glassmakers love it.

nodes/k_charcoal/questions/0/why.en: With little air, the wood can't burn away; it turns into black charcoal.

nodes/k_charcoal/questions/0/answers/0.en: Heating wood with very little air

nodes/k_charcoal/questions/0/answers/1.en: Burning wood in a big, open bonfire

nodes/k_charcoal/questions/1/q.en: Why do smiths use charcoal instead of wood?

nodes/k_charcoal/questions/1/why.en: Charcoal gives a hotter, cleaner fire, which smiths need to work metal.

nodes/k_charcoal/questions/2/q.en: What leaves the wood as it turns into charcoal?

nodes/k_charcoal/questions/2/why.en: Water and smoke escape, and black carbon stays behind.

nodes/k_building/desc.en: A building needs a strong base (foundation) so it doesn't sink, walls to carry the roof, and a sloped roof so rain runs off.

nodes/k_building/page.en: A building needs a strong base, called a foundation, so it doesn't sink. The walls hold up the roof, and a sloped roof lets rain run off. Triangles make a wooden frame stiff. Every door and window needs a strong beam above it.

nodes/k_building/questions/0/why.en: On a slope, rain runs down and away instead of soaking in.

nodes/k_building/questions/0/answers/1.en: So birds can sit on it

nodes/k_building/questions/1/q.en: Which shape makes a wooden frame stiff?

nodes/k_building/questions/1/why.en: A triangle can't be pushed out of shape, so it keeps frames strong.

nodes/k_building/questions/2/q.en: Why does a house need a foundation?

nodes/k_building/questions/2/why.en: The foundation is a strong base that stops the heavy house sinking.

nodes/k_building/questions/2/answers/1.en: So rain runs off the roof

nodes/k_building/questions/2/answers/2.en: So the windows let in light

nodes/k_thatch/desc.en: Thatch is a roof of tightly packed straw or reeds laid in thick layers on a steep roof so rain runs down the outside.

nodes/k_thatch/page.en: Thatch is a roof made of straw or reeds, packed tightly in thick layers. It sits on a steep roof, so rain runs down the outside and the inside stays dry. A good thatched roof lasts many years, and it keeps the house warm in winter.

nodes/k_thatch/questions/0/q.en: Why is a thatched roof built steep?

nodes/k_thatch/questions/0/why.en: On a steep roof, rain slides down the straw before it can soak in.

nodes/k_thatch/questions/0/answers/1.en: So snow can sit on top

nodes/k_thatch/questions/1/why.en: Thatch is thick layers of tightly packed straw or reeds.

nodes/k_thatch/questions/2/q.en: How does thatch help you in winter?

nodes/k_thatch/questions/2/why.en: Thick straw traps warm air, like a cosy blanket on the house.

nodes/k_compost/desc.en: Compost is old plants, straw and manure broken down by tiny living things (bacteria, fungi, worms) into dark crumbly soil food.

nodes/k_compost/page.en: Compost is made when tiny living things, like bacteria, fungi and worms, break down old plants, straw and manure. They turn it all into dark, crumbly food for the soil. The heap needs air and a little water, and turning it with a fork makes it work faster. All their busy work makes the heap warm inside!

nodes/k_compost/questions/0/q.en: Who turns old plants into compost?

nodes/k_compost/questions/0/why.en: Tiny living things eat the old plants and turn them into compost.

nodes/k_compost/questions/1/q.en: Your compost heap is very slow. What can you do?

nodes/k_compost/questions/1/why.en: Turning lets in air, which helps the tiny living things work faster.

nodes/k_compost/questions/1/answers/1.en: Cover it with a stone lid

nodes/k_compost/questions/2/q.en: Why does a compost heap feel warm inside?

nodes/k_compost/questions/2/why.en: As bacteria and fungi break things down, they give off heat.

nodes/k_compost/questions/2/answers/0.en: Tiny living things are busy working

nodes/k_compost/questions/2/answers/2.en: The manure was still warm from the animals

nodes/k_bread/desc.en: Sourdough starter is flour and water where wild yeast lives.

nodes/k_bread/page.en: A sourdough starter is flour and water where wild yeast lives. Yeast is a tiny living thing that eats the sugar in flour and makes bubbles of gas. The bubbles make the dough rise. A hot oven sets the bubbles in place, so the bread is soft inside.

nodes/k_bread/questions/0/q.en: Your bread did not rise. What was missing?

nodes/k_bread/questions/0/why.en: Yeast makes the gas bubbles that puff the dough up.

nodes/k_bread/questions/1/q.en: How does yeast make dough rise?

nodes/k_bread/questions/1/why.en: Yeast eats sugar in the flour and gives off gas, which makes bubbles.

nodes/k_bread/questions/1/answers/1.en: It soaks up all the water

nodes/k_bread/questions/2/q.en: Why is baked bread soft and airy inside?

nodes/k_bread/questions/2/why.en: The hot oven firms the dough around the bubbles, so they stay.

nodes/k_bread/questions/2/answers/2.en: The oven squeezes the air out

nodes/k_stove/desc.en: A stove keeps the fire inside a box with a chimney, so heat goes into the pot and smoke goes outside.

nodes/k_stove/page.en: A stove keeps the fire inside a box with a chimney. The heat goes into the pot, and the smoke goes out through the chimney. A stove uses less wood than an open fire, and it is safer. It is perfect for soups and stews that simmer, which means bubble gently, for a long time.

nodes/k_stove/questions/0/q.en: Where does the smoke from a stove go?

nodes/k_stove/questions/0/why.en: The chimney carries smoke up and out of the house.

nodes/k_stove/questions/1/q.en: Why cook on a stove instead of an open fire?

nodes/k_stove/questions/1/why.en: The boxed-in fire sends its heat into the pot, so less wood is wasted.

nodes/k_stove/questions/1/answers/0.en: It uses less wood and is safer

nodes/k_stove/questions/1/answers/2.en: It needs no fuel or wood at all

nodes/k_stove/questions/2/q.en: Your stew should simmer. What should it do?

nodes/k_stove/questions/2/why.en: To simmer means to bubble gently, so food cooks slowly.

nodes/k_stove/questions/2/answers/0.en: Bubble gently for a long time

nodes/k_stove/questions/2/answers/1.en: Boil very hard for just one minute

nodes/k_cows/desc.en: Cows eat grass and clover and chew it again later (chewing the cud, ruminants with a stomach in four parts).

nodes/k_cows/page.en: Cows eat grass and clover, and their stomach has four parts. Later they bring the food back up and chew it again, which is called chewing the cud. A cow gives milk after she has had a calf. Cows drink lots of water and need a dry barn with bedding.

nodes/k_cows/questions/0/q.en: Your cow is lying down, chewing, with no food nearby. What is she doing?

nodes/k_cows/questions/0/why.en: Cows bring food back up and chew it again; this is chewing the cud.

nodes/k_cows/questions/1/q.en: When does a cow start giving milk?

nodes/k_cows/questions/1/why.en: Like other mothers, a cow makes milk to feed her calf.

nodes/k_cows/questions/1/answers/1.en: As soon as she is born

nodes/k_cows/questions/2/q.en: How many parts does a cow's stomach have?

nodes/k_cows/questions/2/why.en: A cow's stomach has four parts to help break down tough grass.

nodes/k_butter/desc.en: Milk has cream (fat) that rises to the top.

nodes/k_butter/page.en: Fresh milk has cream in it, the fatty part, and it rises to the top. If you shake or churn the cream for a long time, the tiny drops of fat stick together into butter. The thin milk left over is called buttermilk.

nodes/k_butter/questions/0/q.en: Where does the cream go in a pail of fresh milk?

nodes/k_butter/questions/0/why.en: Cream, the fatty part of milk, rises and can be skimmed off the top.

nodes/k_butter/questions/1/q.en: How does churning turn cream into butter?

nodes/k_butter/questions/1/why.en: Shaking makes tiny drops of fat bump together and stick into butter.

nodes/k_butter/questions/1/answers/1.en: The cream gets very cold and hard

nodes/k_butter/questions/2/q.en: What is left over after making butter?

nodes/k_butter/questions/2/why.en: After the butter forms, the thin liquid left behind is buttermilk.

nodes/k_bees/desc.en: Bees collect nectar and pollen from flowers.

nodes/k_bees/page.en: Bees visit flowers to collect sweet nectar and dusty pollen. They carry pollen from flower to flower, which is called pollination, so plants can make fruit and seeds. Bees turn nectar into honey, store it in wax combs, and need water to drink, too.

nodes/k_bees/questions/0/q.en: Why do your apple trees need bees?

nodes/k_bees/questions/0/why.en: Moving pollen between flowers, called pollination, lets plants make fruit and seeds.

nodes/k_bees/questions/0/answers/0.en: Bees carry pollen so fruit can grow

nodes/k_bees/questions/0/answers/2.en: Bees eat the little bugs on the bark

nodes/k_bees/questions/1/q.en: What do bees make honey from?

nodes/k_bees/questions/1/why.en: Bees collect sweet nectar from flowers and turn it into honey.

nodes/k_bees/questions/2/q.en: Where do bees store their honey?

nodes/k_bees/questions/2/why.en: Bees build combs out of wax and fill them with honey.

nodes/k_honey/desc.en: Honeycomb is made of six-sided wax cells filled with honey.

nodes/k_honey/page.en: A honeycomb is made of six-sided wax cells full of honey. Crush the comb and strain it through a cloth: the honey drips out, and the wax stays behind. Beeswax makes candles and keeps things waterproof. Honey keeps for years without going bad.

nodes/k_honey/questions/0/q.en: What shape are the cells in a honeycomb?

nodes/k_honey/questions/0/why.en: Bees build six-sided wax cells that fit snugly together.

nodes/k_honey/questions/1/q.en: How do you get honey out of the comb?

nodes/k_honey/questions/1/why.en: Crushing breaks the cells, and straining lets the honey drip out.

nodes/k_honey/questions/2/q.en: What can you make with the leftover beeswax?

nodes/k_honey/questions/2/why.en: Beeswax makes good candles and can make things waterproof.

nodes/k_salt/desc.en: Salt pulls water out of food, and the tiny germs that spoil food cannot grow without water.

nodes/k_salt/page.en: Food spoils when tiny germs grow in it, and germs need water to grow. Salt pulls the water out of food, so the germs can't grow. That is why salted, dried and pickled foods keep for a long time. Salt comes from the sea or from salt mines.

nodes/k_salt/questions/0/q.en: Why does salted food keep for a long time?

nodes/k_salt/questions/0/why.en: Without water, the germs that spoil food cannot grow.

nodes/k_salt/questions/1/q.en: What do germs need to grow in food?

nodes/k_salt/questions/1/why.en: Germs need water, so taking the water away stops them.

nodes/k_salt/questions/2/why.en: Salt is dried from seawater or dug out of salt mines.

nodes/k_mucking/page.en: Animals make dung, and when it mixes with their old bedding straw we call it muck. Mucking out means cleaning the muck away, and it keeps the animals clean and healthy. Rotted manure is rich food for the fields. What is waste for animals is food for plants!

nodes/k_mucking/questions/0/q.en: Why do you muck out the barn?

nodes/k_mucking/questions/0/why.en: Fresh, clean bedding keeps animals healthy and comfortable.

nodes/k_mucking/questions/1/q.en: What can you do with rotted manure?

nodes/k_mucking/questions/1/why.en: Rotted manure is rich plant food that helps crops grow.

nodes/k_mucking/questions/2/why.en: Muck is animal dung mixed with the old bedding straw.

nodes/k_feed/desc.en: Hens eat grain and seeds, cows and sheep eat grass, clover and hay.

nodes/k_feed/page.en: Hens eat grain and seeds. Cows and sheep eat grass, clover and hay, which is dried grass. Leftover vegetables and oilcake, the pressed seeds left after making oil, can be feed too. Every animal needs clean water, and too much of one food is not healthy.

nodes/k_feed/questions/0/q.en: What do cows and sheep mostly eat?

nodes/k_feed/questions/0/why.en: Cows and sheep eat grass and clover, and hay is dried grass.

nodes/k_feed/questions/1/why.en: After seeds are pressed for oil, the leftover cake makes good feed.

nodes/k_feed/questions/1/answers/0.en: Pressed seeds left after making oil

nodes/k_feed/questions/1/answers/1.en: A sweet cake baked for the farm animals

nodes/k_feed/questions/2/q.en: Why give your animals a mix of foods?

nodes/k_feed/questions/2/why.en: Animals stay healthy with a mix of foods and clean water.

nodes/k_feed/questions/2/answers/0.en: Too much of one food isn't healthy

nodes/k_feed/questions/2/answers/1.en: Mixed food means they need no water

nodes/k_feed/questions/2/answers/2.en: Mixed food is cheaper to buy

nodes/k_rotation/desc.en: Growing the same crop in the same bed again and again tires the soil and invites its pests.

nodes/k_rotation/page.en: Don't grow the same crop in the same bed year after year. The soil gets tired, and that crop's pests move in. Changing the crop each time is called rotation. Beans, peas and clover are special: they put a plant food called nitrogen back into the soil.

nodes/k_rotation/questions/0/why.en: Rotation means growing a different crop in the bed each time.

nodes/k_rotation/questions/0/answers/0.en: Changing the crop in a bed each time

nodes/k_rotation/questions/0/answers/1.en: Turning the soil round and round

nodes/k_rotation/questions/0/answers/2.en: Planting all your crops in a big circle

nodes/k_rotation/questions/1/q.en: Which plants put nitrogen back into the soil?

nodes/k_rotation/questions/1/why.en: Beans, peas and clover add nitrogen, a plant food, to the soil.

nodes/k_rotation/questions/2/q.en: You grow wheat in the same bed every year. What happens?

nodes/k_rotation/questions/2/why.en: One crop again and again tires the soil and feeds the same pests.

nodes/k_rotation/questions/2/answers/0.en: The soil tires and pests move in

nodes/k_rotation/questions/2/answers/1.en: The wheat grows taller each year

nodes/k_seasons/desc.en: The year has spring, summer, autumn and winter because the Earth is tilted as it circles the Sun.

nodes/k_seasons/page.en: The year has four seasons: spring, summer, autumn and winter. They happen because the Earth is tilted, or leaning, as it travels around the Sun. In winter the days are short and cold, so plants grow slowly. Seeds sprout in spring, crops ripen in summer, and we harvest in autumn.

nodes/k_seasons/questions/0/why.en: Because Earth is tilted, our part gets more sunlight in summer and less in winter.

nodes/k_seasons/questions/0/answers/0.en: The Earth leans as it circles the Sun

nodes/k_seasons/questions/0/answers/1.en: The Sun gets bigger in summer

nodes/k_seasons/questions/0/answers/2.en: The Earth gets closer to the Sun in summer

nodes/k_seasons/questions/1/q.en: Why do plants grow slowly in winter?

nodes/k_seasons/questions/1/why.en: Plants need light and warmth, and winter has little of both.

nodes/k_seasons/questions/1/answers/0.en: The days are short and cold

nodes/k_seasons/questions/1/answers/1.en: The soil has no seeds left

nodes/k_seasons/questions/2/q.en: In which season do farmers harvest most crops?

nodes/k_seasons/questions/2/why.en: Crops ripen in summer and are gathered in autumn.

nodes/k_frost/desc.en: Water in the soil freezes and expands in winter, pushing stones upward a little each year (frost heave).

nodes/k_frost/page.en: In winter, water in the soil freezes into ice. Ice takes up more space than water, so it pushes stones up a little every year; this is called frost heave. That is why farmers find new stones every spring. They piled them up to build stone walls and paths.

nodes/k_frost/questions/0/q.en: Why do new stones appear in your field each spring?

nodes/k_frost/questions/0/why.en: Frozen water swells and pushes stones a little higher every winter.

nodes/k_frost/questions/0/answers/1.en: The stones grew bigger over the winter

nodes/k_frost/questions/1/q.en: What happens to water when it freezes?

nodes/k_frost/questions/1/why.en: Ice takes up more room than water, so it pushes soil and stones.

nodes/k_frost/questions/2/q.en: What did farmers do with all those stones?

nodes/k_frost/questions/2/why.en: Farmers piled the stones into walls and paths, so they were useful.

nodes/k_pond/desc.en: A pond collects rain and keeps water for dry days.

nodes/k_pond/page.en: A pond collects rainwater and keeps it for dry days. Ducks, frogs and dragonflies make their homes there. Clay at the bottom holds the water in, because water can't soak through it. Farmers also soak flax stems in ponds to loosen their fibres, which is called retting.

nodes/k_pond/questions/0/q.en: Why does a pond need clay at the bottom?

nodes/k_pond/questions/0/why.en: Water can't soak through clay, so it stays in the pond.

nodes/k_pond/questions/1/q.en: How does a pond help in a dry summer?

nodes/k_pond/questions/1/why.en: A pond stores rainwater, so you still have water when it doesn't rain.

nodes/k_pond/questions/2/q.en: Why soak flax stems in a pond?

nodes/k_pond/questions/2/why.en: Soaking, called retting, loosens the long fibres inside flax stems.

nodes/k_trees/desc.en: Trees grow from seeds or young saplings and take years to grow.

nodes/k_trees/page.en: A tree grows from a seed or from a young tree called a sapling. It takes many years to grow big. In a woodlot, cut just a few trees at a time and plant new ones, so wood never runs out. Once a fruit tree is grown, it gives fruit every year.

nodes/k_trees/questions/0/q.en: How can your woodlot never run out of wood?

nodes/k_trees/questions/0/why.en: Cutting a little and replanting means new trees are always growing.

nodes/k_trees/questions/0/answers/0.en: Cut a few trees and plant new ones

nodes/k_trees/questions/0/answers/1.en: Cut all the trees at once

nodes/k_trees/questions/0/answers/2.en: Only cut the youngest, smallest trees

nodes/k_trees/questions/1/why.en: A sapling is a young tree, ready to be planted out.

nodes/k_trees/questions/2/q.en: Why plant a fruit tree, even though it grows slowly?

nodes/k_trees/questions/2/why.en: Once a fruit tree is grown, it gives a harvest year after year.

nodes/k_iron/desc.en: Iron ore is rock that contains iron.

nodes/k_iron/page.en: Iron ore is a rock with iron hidden inside it. When it is heated very, very hot with charcoal, the iron comes out of the rock; this is called smelting. Hot iron glows and can be hammered into shape. When it cools, iron is hard and strong.

nodes/k_iron/questions/0/why.en: Iron ore is rock that has iron hidden inside.

nodes/k_iron/questions/1/why.en: Smelting uses great heat and charcoal to get iron out of rock.

nodes/k_iron/questions/1/answers/0.en: Heating ore so the iron comes out

nodes/k_iron/questions/1/answers/1.en: Hammering hot iron into new shapes

nodes/k_iron/questions/2/q.en: When is iron easiest to hammer into shape?

nodes/k_iron/questions/2/why.en: Glowing hot iron is soft enough to shape; cold iron is hard.

nodes/k_smithing/desc.en: A smith heats iron until it glows, then shapes it with a hammer on an anvil.

nodes/k_smithing/page.en: A smith heats iron until it glows, then hammers it into shape on an anvil, a heavy iron block. Dipping the hot tool quickly into water is called quenching, and it makes the tool harder. Iron tools last much longer than stone tools.

nodes/k_smithing/questions/0/why.en: The smith lays hot iron on the anvil and hammers it into shape.

nodes/k_smithing/questions/0/answers/0.en: A heavy iron block to hammer on

nodes/k_smithing/questions/0/answers/1.en: A big hammer for hitting iron

nodes/k_smithing/questions/0/answers/2.en: A bucket of cold water for cooling

nodes/k_smithing/questions/1/q.en: Why does a smith dip a hot tool into water?

nodes/k_smithing/questions/1/why.en: Cooling it quickly in water, called quenching, makes the tool harder.

nodes/k_smithing/questions/2/q.en: Why swap your stone axe for an iron one?

nodes/k_smithing/questions/2/why.en: Iron is tough and lasts far longer than stone, which chips and breaks.

nodes/k_nails/page.en: Nails hold wooden boards together. Before people had nails, they cut joints: ends that fit together like puzzle pieces. They held the joints tight with wooden pegs. A saw makes straight, thin planks that are good for building.

nodes/k_nails/questions/0/q.en: How did people join wood before they had nails?

nodes/k_nails/questions/0/why.en: Cut joints fit snugly together, and wooden pegs held them tight.

nodes/k_nails/questions/1/why.en: A nail goes through one board into another and holds them together.

nodes/k_nails/questions/2/q.en: Why use a saw to make planks for building?

nodes/k_nails/questions/2/why.en: Straight, even planks fit together neatly when you build.

nodes/k_wind/desc.en: Moving air (wind) pushes the sails of a windmill round.

nodes/k_wind/page.en: Wind is moving air, and it pushes the sails of a windmill round and round. The sails turn a shaft, which is a long pole, and the shaft drives gears that turn heavy millstones. That way, wind can grind flour or pump water, with no people or animals doing the turning.

nodes/k_wind/questions/0/why.en: Wind is moving air, and it pushes the sails round.

nodes/k_wind/questions/1/q.en: How do the sails turn the heavy millstones?

nodes/k_wind/questions/1/why.en: The sails spin a shaft, and gears pass the turning to the stones.

nodes/k_wind/questions/2/q.en: Why build a windmill instead of grinding by hand?

nodes/k_wind/questions/2/why.en: A windmill uses wind power, so people and animals don't have to turn the stones.

nodes/k_wind/questions/2/answers/0.en: The wind does the hard turning

nodes/k_wind/questions/2/answers/2.en: It grinds best with no wind

nodes/k_irrigation/desc.en: Irrigation brings water to crops through channels or pipes.

nodes/k_irrigation/page.en: Irrigation means bringing water to crops through channels or pipes. Water always flows downhill, so the channel must slope down toward the crops. Watering at the roots wastes less water than splashing the leaves. A watering can with a long spout helps you aim right at the roots.

nodes/k_irrigation/questions/0/q.en: Your field is higher than the pond. Why won't channel water reach it?

nodes/k_irrigation/questions/0/why.en: Water flows downhill, so it can't climb up to a higher field.

nodes/k_irrigation/questions/1/q.en: Where is the best place to pour water on a plant?

nodes/k_irrigation/questions/1/why.en: Water at the roots goes where the plant drinks, with less waste.

nodes/k_irrigation/questions/2/q.en: Why does a watering can have a long spout?

nodes/k_irrigation/questions/2/why.en: The spout lets you pour exactly where the roots are.

nodes/k_irrigation/questions/2/answers/0.en: To aim water at the roots

nodes/k_wool/desc.en: Sheep grow thick wool that is cut off (sheared) once a year, which doesn't hurt them.

nodes/k_wool/page.en: Sheep grow thick wool, and once a year it is cut off. This is called shearing, and it doesn't hurt, just like a haircut. The wool is cleaned, combed and twisted on a spindle into yarn. Spinning turns short, fluffy fibres into long, strong thread.

nodes/k_wool/questions/0/why.en: Wool is like hair, so cutting it off doesn't hurt the sheep.

nodes/k_wool/questions/0/answers/0.en: No, it is like a haircut

nodes/k_wool/questions/1/q.en: What does spinning do to wool?

nodes/k_wool/questions/1/why.en: Twisting short fibres on a spindle joins them into one long, strong yarn.

nodes/k_wool/questions/1/answers/0.en: Makes long thread from short fibres

nodes/k_wool/questions/1/answers/1.en: Washes all the dirt and grease out of it

nodes/k_wool/questions/2/why.en: Sheep grow a thick new coat each year, so they are sheared once a year.

nodes/k_weaving/desc.en: Cloth is woven on a loom: long threads (the warp) are stretched tight and another thread (the weft) goes over and under them, back and forth.

nodes/k_weaving/page.en: Cloth is woven on a loom. Long threads called the warp are stretched tight. Another thread, the weft, goes over and under them, back and forth, back and forth. The tighter the weaving, the stronger the cloth.

nodes/k_weaving/questions/0/q.en: What is stretched tight on the loom?

nodes/k_weaving/questions/0/why.en: The warp is stretched tight first, and the weft weaves through it.

nodes/k_weaving/questions/1/q.en: How does the weft thread move?

nodes/k_weaving/questions/1/why.en: The weft goes over one warp thread and under the next, row after row.

nodes/k_weaving/questions/1/answers/0.en: Over and under, back and forth

nodes/k_weaving/questions/1/answers/2.en: Round and round in little circles

nodes/k_weaving/questions/2/q.en: You want strong cloth for a grain sack. How should you weave?

nodes/k_weaving/questions/2/why.en: Tight weaving packs the threads close, which makes strong cloth.

nodes/k_flax/desc.en: Flax is a plant with long fibres inside its stem.

nodes/k_flax/page.en: Flax is a plant with long fibres inside its stem. The stems are soaked until the fibres come loose, which is called retting. Then the fibres are beaten, combed, spun into thread and woven into linen cloth. Flax seeds give linseed oil.

nodes/k_flax/questions/0/q.en: What cloth is made from flax?

nodes/k_flax/questions/0/why.en: Flax fibres are spun and woven into linen.

nodes/k_flax/questions/1/q.en: Why are flax stems soaked first?

nodes/k_flax/questions/1/why.en: Soaking, or retting, loosens the long fibres from the stem.

nodes/k_flax/questions/1/answers/1.en: To make the seeds inside sprout

nodes/k_flax/questions/2/q.en: What do flax seeds give us?

nodes/k_flax/questions/2/why.en: Flax seeds are pressed to make linseed oil.

nodes/k_press/desc.en: A press squeezes fruit or seeds very hard with a big screw.

nodes/k_press/page.en: A press squeezes fruit or seeds very hard when you turn its big wooden screw. Apples give juice, and sunflower and flax seeds give oil. What is left over, called pomace or oilcake, can feed animals or go on the compost.

nodes/k_press/questions/0/q.en: What comes out when you press apples?

nodes/k_press/questions/0/why.en: Squeezing apples hard pushes out their sweet juice.

nodes/k_press/questions/1/q.en: What can you do with the leftover oilcake?

nodes/k_press/questions/1/why.en: Leftovers from pressing still have goodness, so animals can eat them.

nodes/k_press/questions/2/q.en: How does a press squeeze so hard?

nodes/k_press/questions/2/why.en: Turning a big screw pushes the press down with great force.

nodes/k_press/questions/2/answers/1.en: By heating it in the oven

nodes/k_sugar/desc.en: Sugar beets store sugar in their roots.

nodes/k_sugar/page.en: Sugar beets store sugar in their big roots. Their juice is squeezed out and boiled, so the water goes off as steam and sugar crystals are left behind. Before sugar was common, people sweetened their food mostly with honey.

nodes/k_sugar/questions/0/q.en: Where does a sugar beet store its sugar?

nodes/k_sugar/questions/0/why.en: Sugar beets keep their sugar in their big white roots.

nodes/k_sugar/questions/1/why.en: Boiling drives off the water, leaving sugar crystals behind.

nodes/k_sugar/questions/2/q.en: How did people sweeten food before sugar was common?

nodes/k_sugar/questions/2/why.en: Honey was the main sweetener long before sugar was easy to get.

nodes/k_ferment/desc.en: Fermentation: tiny living things (yeasts and bacteria) change food.

nodes/k_ferment/page.en: Microbes are tiny living things, too small to see, like yeasts and bacteria. Some of them change food in a good way, which is called fermentation. Yeast turns the sugar in apple juice into cider, and bacteria turn milk into yogurt. These good microbes keep the bad ones away, so the food keeps longer.

nodes/k_ferment/questions/0/q.en: What turns apple juice into cider?

nodes/k_ferment/questions/0/why.en: Yeast eats the sugar in apple juice and turns it into cider.

nodes/k_ferment/questions/1/why.en: Friendly bacteria change milk into thick, tangy yogurt.

nodes/k_ferment/questions/2/q.en: Why does fermented food keep longer?

nodes/k_ferment/questions/2/why.en: Friendly microbes fill the food, so spoiling germs can't take over.

nodes/k_ferment/questions/2/answers/0.en: Good microbes keep bad ones away

nodes/k_ferment/questions/2/answers/1.en: It is kept in the hot sun

nodes/k_ferment/questions/2/answers/2.en: All the germs have been boiled away

nodes/k_cheese/desc.en: Cheese: milk is thickened (curdled) with cultures and rennet into curds and whey.

nodes/k_cheese/page.en: To make cheese, you thicken milk with cultures, which are friendly bacteria, and rennet. The milk splits into soft lumps called curds and a watery liquid called whey. The curds are pressed into a round wheel and aged in a cool cellar, which makes the taste stronger. Ten litres of milk make only about one kilo of cheese.

nodes/k_cheese/questions/0/q.en: When milk thickens for cheese, what does it split into?

nodes/k_cheese/questions/0/why.en: The soft lumps are curds, and the watery part is whey.

nodes/k_cheese/questions/1/q.en: How can you make a cheese taste stronger?

nodes/k_cheese/questions/1/why.en: Aging slowly in a cool cellar gives cheese a stronger taste.

nodes/k_cheese/questions/1/answers/0.en: Age it in a cool cellar

nodes/k_cheese/questions/1/answers/1.en: Add lots more water to it

nodes/k_cheese/questions/2/q.en: How much milk makes about one kilo of cheese?

nodes/k_cheese/questions/2/why.en: Most of the milk drains away as whey, so it takes about ten litres.

nodes/k_cellar/desc.en: Cold slows down the germs that spoil food.

nodes/k_cellar/page.en: Cold slows down the germs that spoil food. A cellar dug into the ground stays cool and dark all year, even in summer. Potatoes, carrots, apples and cheese can keep there for months. Cool and dark is the rule!

nodes/k_cellar/questions/0/q.en: Why does food keep longer in a cool cellar?

nodes/k_cellar/questions/0/why.en: Germs that spoil food work much more slowly in the cold.

nodes/k_cellar/questions/1/q.en: Why does a cellar stay cool, even in summer?

nodes/k_cellar/questions/1/why.en: Deep in the ground, the temperature stays cool all year round.

nodes/k_cellar/questions/1/answers/0.en: It is dug into the ground

nodes/k_cellar/questions/1/answers/2.en: It is next to the stove

nodes/k_cellar/questions/2/q.en: Which foods can keep in a cellar for months?

nodes/k_cellar/questions/2/why.en: Hardy foods like potatoes, carrots, apples and cheese last for months in a cellar.

nodes/k_pickling/desc.en: Vinegar is made when bacteria turn cider into acid.

nodes/k_pickling/page.en: Vinegar is made when bacteria turn cider into a sour acid. Vegetables kept in vinegar and salt are called pickles. They don't spoil, because the germs that spoil food can't live in sour acid. People pickled food for the winter and for long trips at sea.

nodes/k_pickling/questions/0/why.en: Special bacteria change cider into sour vinegar.

nodes/k_pickling/questions/0/answers/1.en: Salt is stirred into hot water

nodes/k_pickling/questions/1/why.en: The sour vinegar stops the germs that would spoil the vegetables.

nodes/k_pickling/questions/1/answers/0.en: Spoiling germs can't live in acid

nodes/k_pickling/questions/1/answers/1.en: The jars are kept in the warm sun all day

nodes/k_pickling/questions/2/q.en: Why did sailors take pickles on long sea trips?

nodes/k_pickling/questions/2/why.en: Pickled food doesn't spoil, so it lasts through long voyages.

nodes/k_pickling/questions/2/answers/0.en: Pickles keep for a long time

nodes/k_pickling/questions/2/answers/2.en: Pickles are very light to carry

nodes/k_double_dig/desc.en: Double digging loosens the soil two spade-depths deep and mixes compost in, so roots go deeper and more plants fit.

nodes/k_double_dig/page.en: Double digging means loosening the soil two spade-depths deep and mixing in compost. Then roots can grow deeper, and more plants fit in the bed. It is hard work, but you only do it once. If you never step on the bed, it stays loose for years.

nodes/k_double_dig/questions/0/q.en: How deep do you loosen the soil when double digging?

nodes/k_double_dig/questions/0/why.en: Double digging loosens the soil two spade-blades deep.

nodes/k_double_dig/questions/1/q.en: Why is double digging worth the hard work?

nodes/k_double_dig/questions/1/why.en: Deep, loose soil with compost lets roots go down, so plants can grow closer.

nodes/k_double_dig/questions/1/answers/0.en: Roots go deeper and more plants fit

nodes/k_double_dig/questions/1/answers/1.en: Weeds can never, ever grow there again

nodes/k_double_dig/questions/1/answers/2.en: You never need to water again

nodes/k_double_dig/questions/2/q.en: How do you keep a double-dug bed loose for years?

nodes/k_double_dig/questions/2/why.en: Feet pack the soil hard, so walk on the paths instead.

nodes/k_pests/desc.en: Slugs, caterpillars, mice and birds eat crops.

nodes/k_pests/page.en: Slugs, caterpillars, mice and birds all like to eat our crops. But pests have enemies: ladybirds eat aphids (tiny green bugs), owls and cats catch mice, and ducks gobble up slugs. A garden with many different plants has more of these helpers. And remember, more crops bring more pests.

nodes/k_pests/questions/0/q.en: Slugs are eating your lettuce. Which helper could you bring?

nodes/k_pests/questions/1/why.en: Ladybirds gobble up aphids, tiny bugs that harm plants.

nodes/k_pests/questions/2/q.en: Why grow many different kinds of plants?

nodes/k_pests/questions/2/why.en: Many kinds of plants give homes to ladybirds, birds and other helpers.

nodes/k_pests/questions/2/answers/1.en: They make crops grow twice as fast

nodes/k_steel/desc.en: Steel is iron with a tiny bit of carbon (from charcoal) mixed in.

nodes/k_steel/page.en: Steel is iron with a tiny bit of carbon mixed in, and the carbon comes from charcoal. Steel is harder and springier than iron. It keeps a sharp edge and doesn't break easily. Making steel needs a very hot furnace.

nodes/k_steel/questions/0/why.en: Adding a tiny bit of carbon from charcoal turns iron into steel.

nodes/k_steel/questions/0/answers/0.en: Iron with a tiny bit of carbon

nodes/k_steel/questions/0/answers/1.en: Iron mixed with lots of sand

nodes/k_steel/questions/1/q.en: Why make a knife from steel instead of iron?

nodes/k_steel/questions/1/why.en: Steel is harder and springier, so its edge stays sharp.

nodes/k_steel/questions/2/q.en: Where does the carbon in steel come from?

nodes/k_steel/questions/2/why.en: Charcoal is mostly carbon, and a little mixes into the hot iron.

nodes/k_glass/desc.en: Glass is made by melting sand in a very hot furnace until it flows like honey, then shaping it and letting it cool slowly.

nodes/k_glass/page.en: Glass is made by melting sand, with a little plant ash to help, in a very hot furnace. Melted glass flows like honey, so it can be shaped. Then it must cool slowly, or it may crack. Glass lets light through but keeps the wind and rain out.

nodes/k_glass/questions/0/q.en: What is glass mainly made from?

nodes/k_glass/questions/0/why.en: Sand melted in a very hot furnace becomes glass.

nodes/k_glass/questions/1/q.en: Why must new glass cool slowly?

nodes/k_glass/questions/1/why.en: Cooling too fast can crack glass, so it is cooled slowly.

nodes/k_glass/questions/2/q.en: Why put glass in a window?

nodes/k_glass/questions/2/why.en: Glass is clear, so light comes in while wind and rain stay out.

nodes/k_glass/questions/2/answers/0.en: It lets light in and keeps rain out

nodes/k_glass/questions/2/answers/2.en: It lets the fresh breeze blow through

nodes/k_greenhouse/desc.en: Sunlight shines through glass and warms the air and soil inside.

nodes/k_greenhouse/page.en: In a greenhouse, sunlight shines through the glass and warms the air and soil inside. The glass keeps the warm air in, so plants can grow even when it is cold outside. People grow tender plants there, which are plants that don't like cold. They also start early seedlings in spring.

nodes/k_greenhouse/questions/0/q.en: Why is it warm inside a greenhouse?

nodes/k_greenhouse/questions/0/why.en: Sunlight shines in through the glass, and the glass keeps the warm air inside.

nodes/k_greenhouse/questions/0/answers/0.en: Sun warms it and glass keeps heat in

nodes/k_greenhouse/questions/0/answers/1.en: A fire burns under the floor

nodes/k_greenhouse/questions/0/answers/2.en: The plants breathe out lots of hot air

nodes/k_greenhouse/questions/1/why.en: Tender plants get hurt by cold, so a greenhouse keeps them safe.

nodes/k_greenhouse/questions/1/answers/1.en: Plants that are soft to eat

nodes/k_greenhouse/questions/2/q.en: It is still chilly in early spring. Where can you start seedlings?

nodes/k_greenhouse/questions/2/why.en: A greenhouse is warm and bright, just right for young seedlings.

nodes/k_masonry/desc.en: Bricks are laid in rows with mortar between them, each row overlapping the joints below (a bond) so the wall is strong.

nodes/k_masonry/page.en: Bricks are laid in rows with mortar, a sticky paste that dries hard, between them. Each row overlaps the joins in the row below. This pattern is called a bond, and it makes the wall strong. Brick walls don't burn or rot, and they keep a house warm.

nodes/k_masonry/questions/0/q.en: Why does each row of bricks overlap the row below?

nodes/k_masonry/questions/0/why.en: Overlapping, called a bond, ties the bricks together so the wall stays strong.

nodes/k_masonry/questions/0/answers/2.en: It makes the wall look red

nodes/k_masonry/questions/1/why.en: Mortar is a paste that sticks the bricks together and dries hard.

nodes/k_masonry/questions/2/q.en: Why build with bricks instead of wood?

nodes/k_masonry/questions/2/why.en: Fired clay bricks can't catch fire or rot like wood can.

nodes/k_orchard/desc.en: Fruit trees are pruned in winter: cutting out old and crossing branches lets in light and air so the tree makes better fruit.

nodes/k_orchard/page.en: Fruit trees are pruned, or trimmed, in winter. Cutting out old branches and branches that cross lets light and air into the tree, so it makes better fruit. In spring, bees pollinate the blossoms, and in autumn the apples are ripe.

nodes/k_orchard/questions/0/why.en: With more light and air inside, the tree grows better fruit.

nodes/k_orchard/questions/0/answers/0.en: To let in light and air

nodes/k_orchard/questions/1/q.en: When do you prune fruit trees?

nodes/k_orchard/questions/1/why.en: Fruit trees are pruned in winter, before the spring blossoms come.

nodes/k_orchard/questions/2/q.en: Who helps the apple blossoms turn into apples?

nodes/k_orchard/questions/2/why.en: Bees carry pollen between blossoms, which lets apples grow.

nodes/k_olives/desc.en: Olives straight from the tree are too bitter to eat.

nodes/k_olives/page.en: Olives picked straight from the tree taste far too bitter to eat. They are cured, which means soaked in salty water for weeks, until they taste good. Pressed olives give us olive oil. Olive trees can live for hundreds of years.

nodes/k_olives/questions/0/q.en: Why are fresh olives soaked in salty water?

nodes/k_olives/questions/0/why.en: Weeks of soaking in salty water, called curing, takes the bitterness away.

nodes/k_olives/questions/0/answers/0.en: They are too bitter to eat

nodes/k_olives/questions/0/answers/1.en: They are too sweet to eat

nodes/k_olives/questions/0/answers/2.en: They are too dry to eat

nodes/k_olives/questions/1/q.en: How long can an olive tree live?

nodes/k_olives/questions/1/why.en: Olive trees grow slowly and can live for hundreds of years.

nodes/k_olives/questions/2/q.en: What do you get when you press olives?

nodes/k_olives/questions/2/why.en: Pressing squeezes the oil out of olives.

nodes/k_pasta/desc.en: Pasta is flour and egg (or water) kneaded into a dough, rolled thin and cut.

nodes/k_pasta/page.en: Pasta is flour and egg, or flour and water, kneaded into a dough. Kneading means pressing and folding, and it builds gluten, which makes the dough stretchy. The dough is rolled thin and cut into shapes. Fresh pasta cooks in just a few minutes in boiling water.

nodes/k_pasta/questions/0/why.en: Kneading builds gluten, which makes the dough stretchy.

nodes/k_pasta/questions/1/q.en: What is pasta dough made from?

nodes/k_pasta/questions/1/why.en: Pasta needs just flour and eggs, or flour and water.

nodes/k_pasta/questions/2/q.en: How long does fresh pasta take to cook?

nodes/k_pasta/questions/2/why.en: Fresh pasta is thin, so boiling water cooks it in minutes.

nodes/k_hardwood/desc.en: Hardwoods like oak and beech come from broad-leaved trees that grow slowly.

nodes/k_hardwood/page.en: Hardwoods like oak and beech come from trees with broad, flat leaves, and they grow slowly. Their wood is heavy and strong, so it is good for tools, barrels and machine parts. Softwoods come from conifers, trees with needles and cones like pines, and they grow faster.

nodes/k_hardwood/questions/0/q.en: Why make a barrel from oak?

nodes/k_hardwood/questions/0/why.en: Slow-growing hardwoods like oak make heavy, strong wood.

nodes/k_hardwood/questions/0/answers/0.en: Oak wood is heavy and strong

nodes/k_hardwood/questions/0/answers/2.en: Oak wood is soft and light

nodes/k_hardwood/questions/1/why.en: Softwoods come from conifers, the trees with needles and cones.

nodes/k_hardwood/questions/2/q.en: Which kind of tree grows faster?

nodes/k_hardwood/questions/2/why.en: Conifers like pine grow faster than hardwoods like oak and beech.

nodes/k_deep_soil/desc.en: Humus is the dark, rotted part of soil made from old plants.

nodes/k_deep_soil/page.en: Humus is the dark, rotted part of soil, made from old plants. It holds water like a sponge and feeds plants slowly. In deep soil full of humus, many plants can grow close together.

nodes/k_deep_soil/questions/0/why.en: Humus forms when old plants rot down into dark soil.

nodes/k_deep_soil/questions/1/q.en: How is humus like a sponge?

nodes/k_deep_soil/questions/1/why.en: Humus soaks up water and keeps it for plant roots.

nodes/k_deep_soil/questions/2/q.en: Why can many plants grow close in deep, humus-rich soil?

nodes/k_deep_soil/questions/2/why.en: Deep soil with humus holds lots of water and food for many roots.

nodes/k_deep_soil/questions/2/answers/0.en: There is plenty of water and food

nodes/k_deep_soil/questions/2/answers/1.en: Stones in the soil keep roots warm

nodes/k_mulch/desc.en: Mulch is a blanket of straw, leaves or wood chips on top of the soil.

nodes/k_mulch/page.en: Mulch is a blanket of straw, leaves or wood chips laid on top of the soil. It keeps water in the ground and stops weeds, because they get no light. It protects the soil from frost. Slowly, the mulch rots and turns into humus.

nodes/k_mulch/questions/0/why.en: Under thick mulch, weed seeds get no light, so they can't grow.

nodes/k_mulch/questions/0/answers/1.en: It makes the soil too hot

nodes/k_mulch/questions/0/answers/2.en: It makes the soil too wet

nodes/k_mulch/questions/1/q.en: It's a hot, dry week. How does mulch help?

nodes/k_mulch/questions/1/why.en: Mulch covers the soil like a blanket, so less water dries up.

nodes/k_mulch/questions/1/answers/0.en: It keeps water in the soil

nodes/k_mulch/questions/1/answers/1.en: It makes rain fall more often

nodes/k_mulch/questions/2/q.en: What happens to old mulch over time?

nodes/k_mulch/questions/2/why.en: Mulch slowly rots down and becomes humus that feeds the soil.

nodes/k_dyes/desc.en: Many plants give colour: beets and madder red, onion skins yellow, woad blue.

nodes/k_dyes/page.en: Many plants give colour: madder roots and beets make red, onion skins make yellow, and woad makes blue. You boil the plant in water to make a dye bath, then soak the yarn in it. Adding a fixer, called a mordant, makes the colour stay.

nodes/k_dyes/questions/0/q.en: Which plant gives a blue dye?

nodes/k_dyes/questions/0/why.en: Woad leaves make a blue dye.

nodes/k_dyes/questions/1/q.en: You want yellow yarn. What should you boil?

nodes/k_dyes/questions/1/why.en: Onion skins make a warm yellow dye.

nodes/k_dyes/questions/2/q.en: Your dyed yarn faded when washed. What did you forget?

nodes/k_dyes/questions/2/why.en: A mordant fixes the dye, so the colour stays when washed.

nodes/k_colour_mixing/desc.en: Primary dye colours red, yellow and blue mix into secondary colours: red + yellow = orange, yellow + blue = green, red + blue = purple.

nodes/k_colour_mixing/page.en: Red, yellow and blue are the main dye colours. Mix two of them to make a new colour. Red and yellow make orange, yellow and blue make green, and red and blue make purple. Mix all three together and you get brown.

nodes/k_colour_mixing/questions/0/q.en: Which two dye colours make green?

nodes/k_colour_mixing/questions/0/why.en: Yellow mixed with blue gives green.

nodes/k_colour_mixing/questions/1/q.en: You mix red and blue dye. What colour do you get?

nodes/k_colour_mixing/questions/1/why.en: Red and blue together make purple.

nodes/k_colour_mixing/questions/2/q.en: You pour red, yellow and blue together. What colour now?

nodes/k_colour_mixing/questions/2/why.en: Mixing all three main colours makes brown.

nodes/k_worms/desc.en: Earthworms eat dead leaves and compost and leave behind castings, the richest soil food.

nodes/k_worms/page.en: Earthworms eat dead leaves and compost. What they leave behind is called castings, and it is the richest food for soil. Their tunnels let air and water into the ground. In a worm bin, worms turn kitchen scraps into castings.

nodes/k_worms/questions/0/why.en: Castings are worm droppings, and they are very rich food for plants.

nodes/k_worms/questions/0/answers/0.en: What worms leave behind after eating

nodes/k_worms/questions/0/answers/1.en: Little worm eggs in the soil

nodes/k_worms/questions/1/q.en: How do worm tunnels help your plants?

nodes/k_worms/questions/1/why.en: Tunnels make paths for air and water to reach the roots.

nodes/k_worms/questions/1/answers/0.en: They let air and water in

nodes/k_worms/questions/1/answers/1.en: They catch the slugs at night

nodes/k_worms/questions/2/q.en: What does a worm bin do with kitchen scraps?

nodes/k_worms/questions/2/why.en: Worms eat the scraps and leave castings, a rich food for soil.

nodes/k_seed_saving/desc.en: Heirloom plants grow true from their own seeds: let the best plants flower, collect the dry seeds, keep them cool and dry for next year.

nodes/k_seed_saving/page.en: Heirloom plants are old kinds that grow true from their own seeds: the new plants come out just like the parent. Let your best plants flower, and collect the seeds when they are dry. Keep them cool and dry until next year. Seed libraries share old kinds of seeds, so they don't disappear.

nodes/k_seed_saving/questions/0/q.en: Which plants should you save seeds from?

nodes/k_seed_saving/questions/0/why.en: Seeds from your best plants grow into good plants too.

nodes/k_seed_saving/questions/1/q.en: How should you store saved seeds?

nodes/k_seed_saving/questions/1/why.en: Cool, dry seeds stay healthy until planting time next year.

nodes/k_seed_saving/questions/2/q.en: Why do seed libraries share old seeds?

nodes/k_seed_saving/questions/2/why.en: When many people grow old kinds, those plants stay alive for the future.

nodes/k_seed_saving/questions/2/answers/.en: So old seeds can be thrown away

nodes/k_saffron/desc.en: Saffron comes from the three red threads (stigmas) inside each crocus flower, picked by hand.

nodes/k_saffron/page.en: Saffron comes from a purple crocus flower. Inside each flower are three red threads, called stigmas, and they are picked by hand. It takes about 150 flowers to make just one gram, so saffron is very precious. A pinch colours food a golden yellow.

nodes/k_saffron/questions/0/q.en: Why does saffron cost so much?

nodes/k_saffron/questions/0/why.en: About 150 flowers, all picked by hand, make just one gram.

nodes/k_saffron/questions/0/answers/2.en: It grows on big, tall trees

nodes/k_saffron/questions/1/q.en: Which part of the crocus is saffron?

nodes/k_saffron/questions/1/why.en: Saffron is the three red threads, called stigmas, in each flower.

nodes/k_saffron/questions/2/q.en: What does a pinch of saffron do to rice?

nodes/k_saffron/questions/2/why.en: Just a pinch of saffron turns food a golden yellow.

nodes/k_master_baking/desc.en: Fine flour is ground twice and sifted for light cakes.

nodes/k_master_baking/page.en: For light cakes, flour is ground twice and sifted until it is very fine. Beating eggs traps tiny air bubbles. Creaming, or beating, butter and sugar together makes a cake soft. The oven must be evenly hot, not too hot, so the inside bakes before the outside burns.

nodes/k_master_baking/questions/0/q.en: Why beat the eggs for a cake?

nodes/k_master_baking/questions/0/why.en: Beaten eggs hold air, which makes the cake light.

nodes/k_master_baking/questions/0/answer.en: To warm them up for the oven

nodes/k_master_baking/questions/1/q.en: Your cake burned outside but stayed raw inside. Why?

nodes/k_master_baking/questions/1/why.en: Steady, gentle heat lets the middle bake before the outside burns.

nodes/k_master_baking/questions/1/answer.en: The eggs were beaten too long

nodes/k_master_baking/questions/2/q.en: How do you make flour fine enough for light cakes?

nodes/k_master_baking/questions/2/why.en: Grinding twice and sifting makes very fine flour for light cakes.

nodes/k_master_baking/questions/2/answer.en: Grind it twice and sift it
Mix in plenty of coarse bran

nodes/k_wind_pump/desc.en: A wind pump uses the turning sails to move a pump rod up and down, lifting water from deep underground into a tank, day and night whenever the wind blows — without anyone pumping by hand..

nodes/k_wind_pump/page.en: A wind pump uses its turning sails to move a pump rod up and down. Each stroke lifts water from deep underground into a tank. It works day and night, whenever the wind blows, with nobody pumping by hand.

nodes/k_wind_pump/questions/0/q.en: What makes a wind pump work?

nodes/k_wind_pump/questions/0/why.en: The wind spins the sails, and that drives the pump.

nodes/k_wind_pump/questions/1/q.en: How does a wind pump lift water?

nodes/k_wind_pump/questions/1/why.en: The sails move a pump rod up and down, lifting water each time.

nodes/k_wind_pump/questions/1/answers/0.en: A rod moves up and down

nodes/k_wind_pump/questions/2/q.en: When does a wind pump fill the tank?

nodes/k_wind_pump/questions/2/why.en: It runs whenever there is wind, even at night.

nodes/k_living_soil/desc.en: A spoonful of healthy soil holds billions of tiny living things — bacteria, fungi, worms.

nodes/k_living_soil/page.en: Healthy soil is alive! One spoonful holds billions of tiny living things, like bacteria and fungi, and worms live there too. Fungi grow long, thin threads that help roots find water. Feed the soil with compost and don't dig it too much, and it stays alive.

nodes/k_living_soil/questions/0/q.en: How many tiny living things are in a spoonful of healthy soil?

nodes/k_living_soil/questions/0/why.en: Healthy soil is packed with billions of tiny living things.

nodes/k_living_soil/questions/1/q.en: How do fungi help plant roots?

nodes/k_living_soil/questions/1/why.en: Long, thin fungus threads reach far and help roots get water.

nodes/k_living_soil/questions/1/answers/.en: Their threads help roots find water
They scare away the slugs and snails

nodes/k_living_soil/questions/2/q.en: How can you keep your soil alive?

nodes/k_living_soil/questions/2/why.en: Compost feeds the soil life, and too much digging disturbs it.

nodes/k_living_soil/questions/2/answers/.en: Add compost and dig only a little

items/charcoal/desc.de: Langsam verbrannte Holzscheite. Brennstoff für Schmiede und Glasofen.

items/iron_ore/desc.en: Only from the Raw Materials Merchant (unlocked by a dish).
items/iron_ore/desc.de: Nur beim Rohstoffhändler (freigeschaltet durch ein Gericht).

items/iron/desc.en: Smelted ore. The iron age starts here.
items/iron/desc.de: Geschmolzenes Erz. Hier beginnt die Eisenzeit.

items/nails/desc.en: 1 iron bar → 4 nails. Every serious wooden build needs them.
items/nails/desc.de: 1 Eisenbarren → 4 Nägel. Jeder richtige Holzbau braucht sie.

items/steel/desc.en: Iron refined with lots of charcoal. Top-tier tools and machines.
items/steel/desc.de: Eisen, mit viel Holzkohle veredelt. Für die besten Werkzeuge und Maschinen.

items/glass/desc.en: Windows for the Farmhouse, panes for the Greenhouse.
items/glass/desc.de: Fenster für das Bauernhaus, Scheiben für das Gewächshaus.

items/hardwood/desc.en: Dense oak for machine parts. Bought, later grown at the Lumbermill.
items/hardwood/desc.de: Dichtes Eichenholz für Maschinenteile. Gekauft, später aus dem Sägewerk.

items/clay_jar/desc.en: Fired clay jar. Pickles, jam, olives and the fermenter need them.
items/clay_jar/desc.de: Gebrannter Tonkrug. Für Eingelegtes, Marmelade, Oliven und den Gärtopf.

items/ash/desc.en: Burnt weeds and twigs. The first fertilizer: worth 1 point.
items/ash/desc.de: Verbranntes Unkraut und Zweige. Der erste Dünger: 1 Punkt wert.

items/compost/desc.en: Worth 2 fertilizer points. Hungry crops need 1 compost each. Made from straw/weeds, much faster with manure.
items/compost/desc.de: 2 Düngerpunkte wert. Hungrige Pflanzen brauchen je 1 Kompost. Aus Stroh und Unkraut, mit Mist viel schneller.

items/worm_castings/desc.en: Worth 4 fertilizer points. Worms turn compost and straw into the richest soil.
items/worm_castings/desc.de: 4 Düngerpunkte wert. Würmer machen aus Kompost und Stroh die allerbeste Erde.

items/manure/desc.en: From cows and sheep. Makes compost much faster.
items/manure/desc.de: Von Kühen und Schafen. Macht Kompost viel schneller.

items/oilcake/desc.en: Left over after pressing sunflower seeds. Animal feed or compost.
items/oilcake/desc.de: Bleibt beim Pressen von Sonnenblumenkernen übrig. Tierfutter oder Kompost.

items/beeswax/desc.de: Aus Honigwaben. Für Kerzen, zum Abdichten und Polieren.

items/tin_pot/desc.en: The one thing that survived. Needed (not used up) for campfire cooking.
items/tin_pot/desc.de: Das Einzige, was das Feuer überstanden hat. Zum Kochen am Lagerfeuer nötig (wird nicht verbraucht).

items/sourdough_starter/desc.en: Made once, never used up: bread needs it present.
items/sourdough_starter/desc.de: Wird einmal angesetzt und nie verbraucht: Brot braucht ihn nur in der Nähe.

items/yogurt_culture/desc.en: Bought once from the Culture Specialist; kept alive by every batch.
items/yogurt_culture/desc.de: Einmal beim Kulturen-Händler gekauft; jede Ladung hält sie am Leben.

items/cheese_culture/desc.en: Bought once from the Culture Specialist (plant-based rennet).

items/saffron_corm/desc.en: Rare seed, bartered from the Import Broker.

items/rainbow_carrot_seed/desc.en: Rare seed, bartered from the Import Broker.

items/golden_beet_seed/desc.en: Rare seed, bartered from the Import Broker.

items/woad_seed/desc.en: Rare seed, bartered from the Import Broker.

items/feather/desc.en: Hens drop them. Pillows, the library feather duster, the scarecrow's hat.
items/feather/desc.de: Hühner verlieren sie. Für Kissen, den Staubwedel der Bücherei und den Hut der Vogelscheuche.

items/feed_mash/desc.en: Old vegetables chopped with straw — or food that went stale at the change of season. Hens, cows and sheep eat it; the compost takes it too.
items/feed_mash/desc.de: Altes Gemüse mit Stroh zerhackt — oder Essen, das beim Jahreszeitenwechsel alt geworden ist. Hühner, Kühe und Schafe fressen es; der Kompost nimmt es auch.

items/linseed/desc.en: Flax seeds. Pressed for linseed oil, or fed to hens.
items/linseed/desc.de: Flachssamen. Werden zu Leinöl gepresst oder an Hühner verfüttert.

items/linseed_oil/desc.en: Oils tools, looms and wood. (Not for frying.)
items/linseed_oil/desc.de: Ölt Werkzeug, Webstühle und Holz. (Nicht zum Braten.)

items/quartz/desc.en: Sometimes hiding in a stone. Pretty, and the market pays well.
items/quartz/desc.de: Versteckt sich manchmal in einem Stein. Hübsch, und der Markt zahlt gut dafür.

items/relic/desc.en: An arrowhead, an old coin, a fossil… found while weeding. Goes in the album, or sell it.
items/relic/desc.de: Eine Pfeilspitze, eine alte Münze, ein Fossil… beim Jäten gefunden. Kommt ins Album, oder du verkaufst es.

items/honey_cake/desc.en: A cake sweetened with honey instead of sugar.
items/honey_cake/desc.de: Ein Kuchen, der mit Honig statt mit Zucker gesüßt ist.

meta/seasons/mods/summer/abundance.de: Die Bienen fliegen den ganzen Tag: +30% Honigwaben.

meta/seasons/mods/autumn/abundance.en: Fruit and nuts: orchard +40%; branches fall (sticks ×2).
meta/seasons/mods/autumn/abundance.de: Obst und Nüsse: Obstgarten +40%; Äste fallen herunter (Stöcke ×2).

meta/seasons/mods/winter/abundance.en: Frost brings stones up (pick them for walls); indoor work by the fire −10% energy; wool grows thick.
meta/seasons/mods/winter/abundance.de: Der Frost drückt Steine nach oben (sammle sie für Mauern); Arbeit drinnen am Feuer −10% Energie; die Wolle wächst dick.

meta/luck/events/0/text.en: A lost coin in the weeds!

meta/luck/events/2/text.en: A four-leaf clover! You feel lucky.
meta/luck/events/2/text.de: Ein vierblättriges Kleeblatt! Du hast Glück.

meta/luck/events/3/text.en: Something old in the soil: a relic for the album!
meta/luck/events/3/text.de: Etwas Altes in der Erde: ein Fundstück fürs Album!

meta/luck/events/4/text.en: A sparkling quartz crystal inside a stone!
meta/luck/events/4/text.de: Ein glitzernder Quarzkristall in einem Stein!

meta/luck/events/5/text.en: It rained: no watering needed, and the well fills a little.
meta/luck/events/5/text.de: Es hat geregnet: kein Gießen nötig, und der Brunnen füllt sich ein bisschen.

meta/luck/events/10/text.en: A neighbour drops off a little gift basket.
meta/luck/events/10/text.de: Ein Nachbar bringt einen kleinen Geschenkkorb vorbei.

meta/luck/events/11/text.en: The seed merchant adds one for free.
meta/luck/events/11/text.de: Der Samenhändler legt einen gratis dazu.

meta/luck/events/12/text.en: A golden acorn glints under a leaf!
meta/luck/events/12/text.de: Unter einem Blatt glänzt eine goldene Eichel!

meta/giftCards/pool/9/desc.de: Das Glück von Nachbarschaftshilfen hält 15 Fragen länger.

meta/perks/list/0/desc.en: Butterflies flutter over your fields. A thank-you from Granny Maud's meadow.
meta/perks/list/0/desc.de: Schmetterlinge flattern über deinen Feldern. Ein Dankeschön von Oma Mauds Wiese.

meta/perks/list/1/desc.en: Sparkles where you tap the farm. A trick the twins taught you.
meta/perks/list/1/desc.de: Es funkelt, wo du auf den Hof tippst. Ein Trick, den dir die Zwillinge beigebracht haben.

meta/perks/list/2/desc.en: A jingle when you sell, a pop when you harvest, a chime for new things. Ella's little bell started it.
meta/perks/list/2/desc.de: Ein Klimpern beim Verkaufen, ein Plopp beim Ernten, ein Glöckchen für neue Dinge. Angefangen hat es mit Ellas kleiner Glocke.

meta/perks/list/3/desc.en: A rainbow over the farm after the rain. Hilde says the washing dries best under one.
meta/perks/list/3/desc.de: Ein Regenbogen über dem Hof nach dem Regen. Hilde sagt, darunter trocknet die Wäsche am besten.

meta/perks/list/4/desc.en: Quick Rest sums sometimes crackle with lightning.
meta/perks/list/4/desc.de: Schnelle Rechnungen beim Ausruhen knistern manchmal mit einem Blitz.

meta/perks/list/5/desc.en: A flame counts your quick Rest sums in a row.
meta/perks/list/5/desc.de: Eine Flamme zählt deine schnellen Rechnungen hintereinander.

meta/perks/list/6/desc.en: Coins fly into your purse when you sell.
meta/perks/list/6/desc.de: Beim Verkaufen fliegen Münzen in deinen Geldbeutel.

meta/perks/list/7/desc.en: Confetti when you harvest everything at once.
meta/perks/list/7/desc.de: Konfetti, wenn du alles auf einmal erntest.

meta/perks/list/8/desc.en: Blossom petals in spring, leaves in autumn, snowflakes in winter.
meta/perks/list/8/desc.de: Blütenblätter im Frühling, Blätter im Herbst, Schneeflocken im Winter.

meta/postcards/news/goals.en: all your work on the farm ({n} jobs done!)
meta/postcards/news/goals.de: all deiner Arbeit auf dem Hof ({n} Aufgaben erledigt!)

meta/postcards/messages/0.en: Dear {player}, I heard about {news}! Here is a little something for your farm.
meta/postcards/messages/0.de: Hallo {player}, ich habe von {news} gehört! Hier ist eine kleine Überraschung für deinen Hof.

meta/postcards/messages/1.en: Hello {player}! Word travels fast in our village — {news}! I wanted to send you a present.
meta/postcards/messages/1.de: Hallo {player}! Im Dorf spricht sich alles schnell herum — ich habe von {news} gehört! Ich wollte dir ein Geschenk schicken.

meta/postcards/messages/2.en: {player}, everyone is talking about {news}. Thank you again for your help — this is for you!
meta/postcards/messages/2.de: {player}, alle reden von {news}. Danke nochmal für deine Hilfe — das ist für dich!

meta/postcards/messages/3.en: Dear {player}, I was so happy to hear about {news}. I hope this helps on the farm!
meta/postcards/messages/3.de: Hallo {player}, ich habe mich so gefreut, von {news} zu hören. Ich hoffe, das hilft dir auf dem Hof!
